previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted with two weeks of dyspnea, orthopnea, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. Initial evaluation revealed a moderate to large pericardial effusion with signs of early tamponade, bilateral pleural effusions, and leukocytosis. She underwent pericardiocentesis, draining 640 cc of serosanguinous fluid, after which her symptoms improved. A CT scan with contrast was performed but led to an anaphylactic reaction, requiring epinephrine and close monitoring; she recovered fully. The pericardial fluid showed no malignancy or infection, and the etiology remained unclear. She was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with levofloxacin and managed for acute on chronic diastolic heart failure with continued diuresis. Her shoulder pain, previously attributed to musculoskeletal causes, improved post-procedure. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to avoid iodinated contrast, monitor weight, restart atorvastatin, discontinue potassium and valsartan temporarily, and follow up with primary care and cardiology.

Brief Hospital Course:
Pt is a ___ yo F with hx of of CAD s/p PCI in ___, pericardial

HTN, breast cancer, thyroglossal cyst and diastolic CHF who

# Chest pain - Pain is sharp and midsternal, per patient similar 
to the pain she had when admitted with pericardial effusion last 
month. She has acute on chronic diastolic CHF with EF 55% on TTE 
1 month ago, with clinical symptoms of progressive CHF over past 
few months. She had a pericardial effusion of unkown etiology 
last month, and currently undergoing work-up for malignancy. She 
was slightly volume overloaded on exam on admission and CXR 
showed new vascular congestion. Bedside U/S in the ED did not 
show pericardial effusion and no pulsus on exam. She was ruled 
out for MI with negative enzymes and ECG showed non-specific T 
wave changes. She was monitored on telemetry without events. 
Patient is on lasix 40mg PO daily at home and this dose was 
doubled with goal output 1L negative daily. Patient's chest pain 
and breathing improved with diuresis and ibuprofen. Given recent 
effusion, there was concern for possible constrictive 
pericarditis and TTE was repeated. It showed small effusion 
similar to prior likely inflammatory or blood/cellular elements. 
There was some evidence of mild diastolic dysfunction, but no 
hemodynamic instability. Patient was discharged with 40mg PO 
lasix twice daily and advised to weigh herself frequently. She 
is being followed by orthopedics for left shoulder pain thought 
to be due to left outlet impingement which may also be causing 
referred pain, she was given ibuprofen for this. Patient will 
continue to outpatient workup of possible malignancy given the 
initial etiology of her effusion is not yet clear.
.
# UTI - positive U/A on admission, patient asymptomatic but 
reports increased vaginal dryness recently. She was treated for 
a simple UTI with a 3-day course of ciprofloxacin.

___. Pt had new TWI in V2-3 on initial ECG which reverted to 
baseline on susbequent ECG, and overall non-specific ST-T 
changes. She was ruled out for ACS on admission. Her chest pain 
as above is atypical though may be related to the small 
remaining effusion, or musculoskeletal in etiology. She was 
continued on her aspirin and statin and blood pressure regimen, 
with increased lasix dosing as above.
.
# HTN - normotensive throughout hospitalization. She has 
recently discontinued one of her medications (mitolazone) due to 
dizziness at home. She had no evidence of orthostasis throughout 
admission and tolerated increased dose of lasix well. Also 
continued on home dose amlodipine.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,
  
You were admitted with chest pain and difficulty breathing. Your 
chest x-ray showed mild accumulation of fluid in your lungs. Lab 
tests revealed that you were not having a heart attack. A 
bedside ultrasound did not show any fluid accumulation around 
your heart, and we repeated an echo which showed some mild fluid 
that is unchanged from your discharge a few weeks ago. We 
recommend that you increase your lasix dose to 40mg twice a day 
in order to keep your fluid from reaccumulating in your lungs. 
You have follow-up appointments with several physicians to 
continue the work-up for why you had fluid around your heart in 
the first place. You should go to physical therapy for your 
shoulder pain as recommended by your orthopedist.
  
Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.
  
We also found that you had a mild urinary tract infection on 
admission which we are treating with a 3-day course of 
antibiotics, see below.
  
We have made the following changes to your medications:

food
